## Overview

The Sinixt, also known as the Sin-Aikst, Sin Aikst, Senijextee, Arrow Lakes Band, or Lakes, are a First Nations people of Salishan linguistic extraction. Their traditional territory extends along the Columbia River, Arrow Lakes, Slocan Valley, and parts of Kootenay Lake, in what are now British Columbia and Eastern Washington. Today they live primarily on the Colville Indian Reservation in Washington, where they form part of the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation, while a permanent Sinixt presence also continues in the Slocan Valley. The Sinixt speak a dialect of the Colville-Okanagan language known as snsəlxcín or n̓səl̓xčin̓. Their folk-culture significance lies in seasonal fishing, hunting, gathering, pithouse settlement, distinctive canoe construction, salmon practices, place-based law, oral teaching, and continuing efforts to preserve language and cultural responsibilities.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

They do record that girls learned plant lore and tanning.

### Architecture

Sinixt winter settlement included warm, semi-subterranean houses, and archaeological evidence identifies large pithouses in the Slocan Valley. Some had diameters of over 20 metres (66 feet), while the Slocan Narrows site included some of the most recent very large pithouses. The sources describe these houses as part of a socially and economically complex society. Major hydroelectric projects along the Columbia and Kootenay rivers flooded many graveyards and village sites, limiting excavation and study. The largely Sinixt community of Inchelium, Washington, on the banks of the Columbia, was also engulfed by rising waters from the dam and had to be relocated.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They do describe a distinctive Sturgeon-nosed canoe, about 15–17 feet (4.5–5 meters) long, with a cedar frame covered by large slabs of pine bark. It rode low in the water and had downward-sloping tips to reduce wind resistance. Sinixt hunters also used bows and arrows, canoes, fishing gear, baskets on poles, and spears with detachable tips like a harpoon.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Early white explorers reported that Sinixt people were of average height and size and had hazel eyes, but the sources do not present this as a system of adornment.

## Music & performance

The sources document dances associated with fishing-season relationships between the Sinixt and Colville people. At Kettle Falls, the Colville people celebrated the Sinixt arrival during fishing season with a three-day dance, and the tribes held a three-day dance at the end of their season. These performances were connected to salmon fishing and intertribal relations.

The sources also identify live music and performance as features of the annual Barter Fair held every fall in Vallican, B.C. The event encourages local bartering of goods and services. Northern Sinixt also host Sinixt Radio on Nelson, B.C. Community Radio station CJLY-FM.

## Dance & theatre

The sources name a three-day dance associated with the Sinixt arrival at Kettle Falls during fishing season and another three-day dance held at the end of the season. The annual Barter Fair in Vallican includes live music and performance.

## Festivals & rituals

Sinixt seasonal life was organized around fishing, hunting, gathering, and movement between ecological zones. Summers were spent fishing, hunting, and gathering food in a mountain- and lake-dominated homeland, while winter was spent in more sheltered valleys. Starting in June, mature salmon arrived at Kettle Falls. The Sinixt caught salmon that were not strong enough to clear the falls, allowing the strongest fish to continue upstream to spawn. Both bands travelled to Red Mountain near Rossland, B.C. to harvest huckleberries in August. Hunting took place in late autumn, although food shortages often occurred by late winter.

Children were closely monitored by elders. At about six years of age, they began learning tribal legends, family history, tribal ways, and tribal laws. At eight or nine, they learned to swim and run long distances; boys learned to make and use weapons and fishing gear, while girls learned plant lore, tanning, care of young children, maintenance of dwellings, and meal preparation. Children also undertook short excursions to seek protective spirits and were expected to return with an object proving that they had made the journey. The sources describe customs related to pregnancy, birth, education, and funerals.

## Foodways

Sinixt staples included huckleberry, salmon, and roots such as camas and bitterroot. Other foods included black moss, serviceberry, gooseberry, foam berry, hazelnuts, wild carrots, peppermint, deer, elk, moose, caribou, rabbit, mountain sheep, mountain goat, and bear. After acquiring horses, the Sinixt also travelled east to hunt bison. Pine pitch was chewed like gum, and the sources mention a range of herbal medicines.

Fishing was especially important. Mature salmon reached Kettle Falls beginning in June, and the Sinixt selected fish unable to clear the falls so that stronger salmon could continue to spawn. The Lower Sinixt used baskets on poles and spears with detachable tips. They continued to elect a Salmon Chief until the construction of Grand Coulee Dam ended the great salmon runs and caused a severe shortage of food.

## Oral tradition & literature

Sinixt children learned tribal legends and family history from about six years of age. Oral accounts also preserved memories of epidemics, territorial relations, seasonal practices, and the powers associated with the sun, stars, water, salmon, coyote, and other animals. Children undertook journeys to seek protective spirits, and each person was expected to acquire multiple spirits because each had different powers.

Sharon Montgomery of the Nakusp Museum and tribal legend recorded by Nancy Perkins Wynecoop and Nettie Wynecoop Clark describe the Sinixt as the “Mother Tribe” of the Pacific Northwest Salish, although contributors to the article’s forum disputed these claims as lacking ethnographic or historical foundation. Eva Orr’s teaching is associated with “keeping the Lakes’ way,” a moral code emphasizing reciprocal relationships between humans, the land, and the realm of spirits in which ancestors dwell. In 2021, Smum iem and Maa Press Publishing and Distribution created a map of Sinixt təmxʷúlaʔxʷ, or territory, with place names labeled in Snsəlxcín.

## Language & religion

Sinixt is a distinct dialect of the Colville-Okanagan language and belongs to the Southern Interior Salish subgroup of the Salishan language family. The dialect is associated primarily with the Columbia River Basin and is closely related to other Interior Salish languages and dialects. As of 2022, it had around 30 first-language speakers. Six tribes of the Colville Confederated Tribes speak Sinixt: the suknaqínx, sn̓ʕay̓ckstx, mətxʷu, nspil̓m̓, sn̓pʕaw̓ilx, and sx̌ʷy̓iłpx.

The sources state that Sinixt religion was mainly concerned with harnessing power. The sun, stars, water, and different animals, especially salmon and coyote, each had different powers. The whole tribe was led by one head chief, ilmi wm, while smaller villages had local chiefs called “thinkers.” Sinixt society was matrilocal, with newly married couples living with the wife’s family. The sources also describe Catholic conversion among some Sinixt during the nineteenth century, including Kin-Ka-Nawha.
